title: Labor
logline: Labor Day weekend: Theo kidnaps half of Delgado Hall to his father’s beach house in Malibu, where the gumbo takes an hour, the father takes six minutes, and somebody has to explain the dignity of labor.

previously.text: Adrian Hale told the seminar your belief in a soul is just an inheritance. You told him he’d inherited his atheism too.
Then he paired you with Lena for the semester. Her red ink in your margin: *Cite me.*
She told you about Wes — the boat, the storm, sixteen. You told her you’d been worried she had bad taste.
You offered her the whole pack. She said she collects them one at a time — and that she’d need a container.
You took a job washing dishes on the harbor, and a loan from Theo, payable in pie.
Under a full moon, Theo said Los Angeles was three hours away. You told him you couldn’t afford it.

body: Jack wakes to the smell of espresso, which in 412 means Theo is up and something has been decided without him. Fog lies flat and white against the window. Under it the radiator ticks at its own pace, for its own reasons. Jack is in the Browns T-shirt he sleeps in, the helmet on the chest cracked to a ghost by the Glenwood Avenue dryer, and he is cold the way the Central Coast does cold in September: damp, polite, right through.

body.text: The Mooney hoodie is two floors down, being slept in by a redhead.
body.else: The Mooney hoodie is on the chair across the room, which at this hour might as well be Akron.

body: Theo is standing at the foot of the bed. He is dressed — the gray T-shirt with the hole in it, jeans that cost more than they admit to, sunglasses pushed up into the blond — and he has a cortado in each hand from the machine nobody may touch, and the keys to the SL hooked on one finger. He holds a cup out. “I’m making an exception,” he says. “I’m a forgiving man.” Jack takes it. It is the first thing that has ever come out of that machine and into his hands, and it is very good, which feels like the opening move of a con.

“You told me you couldn’t afford LA,” Theo says. “I listened. I’m a wonderful listener; it’s a curse. So I am not taking you to LA.” He waits exactly long enough for Jack’s shoulders to come down. “I’m taking you to *Malibu*.”

Then he pitches it, pacing the eleven feet of 412 like a producer walking a room of executives toward a yes they don’t know they’ve already said. “Picture it. Eight a.m. I knock on two-seventeen. Price opens the door in a sleep mask and says yes before I finish the word. I got as far as *Mal*. Price calls Margot, because Margot is the only person in Delgado who admits to being up at eight. Margot calls Tran, because Tran has a van and a conscience, and Tran is afraid of her, which I respect. Pruitt the Destroyer has a raid tonight and sends his regrets in Elvish.” He sips. “Your Broussard says she has a paper.” “Then she has a paper.” “Nobody has a paper on Labor Day weekend, Costigan. It’s the one weekend the paper gets off. Bring a swimsuit and lowered expectations.”

Theo slides the sunglasses down onto his nose. “Also, I already bought the gas, and gas is — ” “Non-refundable.” Theo points at him with the cup, moved. “You *listen*.”

response: Theo, who has seen the UCen receipt and the face Jack made at it, doesn’t argue, and that’s how Jack knows he planned for it. “Fine. Pay Kevin. It’s his mother’s gas.” He considers this. “Kevin is going to make a spreadsheet. Let him have it. It’s a holiday.”

choices.text: “Put it under the pie.”
response: Theo crosses to the espresso machine, peels off the Post-it — *IOU 1 PIE (TBD) —J.C.* — and writes a second line under it in his unexpectedly neat hand: *+ 1 MALIBU —T.V.* He sticks it back and smooths it flat with his thumb. “The ledger grows,” he says. “I love a ledger. Nobody in my family keeps one.”

choices.text: “Your father’s dishes are mine all weekend. That’s the deal.”
response: “We have a housekeeper.” “Not this weekend you don’t.” Theo laughs, then stops laughing, takes out the iPhone and scrolls through something with a small frown. “…Inés is off till Tuesday.” He looks up. “How did you know that?” “I didn’t,” Jack says, and drinks the cortado. “But it’s Labor Day. Somebody’s housekeeper is always off on Labor Day.”

choices.text: “Malibu’s in LA County, Theo.”
response: “Barely,” Theo says. “Spiritually, it’s in escrow.” He takes the Post-it pad off the desk, draws the coast in four strokes, puts an X at the far left edge of Los Angeles County and labels it *NOT LA (LEGALLY)*, and sticks it to Jack’s forehead. “Pack. You have eleven minutes, and one of them is for your hair.”

body: The Anacapa lot at 9:14 is fog and gulls and the low-tide smell of the Lagoon. Theo has the SL’s top down in the fog on principle, and Vampire Weekend comes thin and bright out of the cassette adapter: a boy begging another boy to get out of Cape Cod tonight. It sounds like a getaway, which is the point.

Kevin is loading his mother’s Odyssey like it’s an ambulance: a cooler, a case of Arrowhead, a first-aid kit with TRAN on the lid in label tape. Gray quarter-zip. A rosary hangs from the mirror, wooden beads and a little medal of a crowned Madonna holding a child. “Our Lady of La Vang,” Kevin says, when he catches Jack looking. “My parish. My mom’s van. They’re both watching.” He hands Jack an index card in a plastic sleeve. He has made one for everybody, with everybody’s numbers on the back; the ones he didn’t have he got off Laney’s phone.

body: Margot arrives in black and oxblood Docs with a canvas tote of books, Barbara Ehrenreich’s *Nickel and Dimed* on top. “Labor Day reading.” “I’m here as an observer. If anyone asks, I wasn’t on this trip. I was *studying* it.”

body.text: Laney comes across the lot in Jack’s Mooney hoodie and very little else he can see, big sunglasses, pulling three suitcases for two nights. “One’s just shoes,” she tells Kevin, who has not asked. “Don’t look at me like that. Shoes are *luggage*.”
body.else: Laney comes across the lot in a sundress and big sunglasses, pulling three suitcases for two nights. “One’s just shoes,” she tells Kevin, who has not asked. “Don’t look at me like that. Shoes are *luggage*.”

body: Lena comes last. White Keds, the OCTAVIA BOOKS tote over one shoulder, a Greek grammar held flat against her chest like a passport. She stops ten feet short of the van. “I’m not going.” “She packed last night,” Laney tells the parking lot. “She packed *twice*.”

body.text: Lena doesn’t look at Jack. She looks at Laney — the look from the curb outside Pi Lam on Friday — and says, “Somebody has to be your person in Malibu.” Then she puts the tote in the van herself, as if it had been her idea all along, which by the time she’s let go of the strap it has been.
body.else: Lena doesn’t look at Jack. She looks at Laney and says, “Somebody has to keep you out of the ocean.” Then she puts the tote in the van herself, as if it had been her idea all along, which by the time she’s let go of the strap it has been.

body: While Kevin checks the tire pressure — he actually checks the tire pressure — she goes into the Odyssey’s glove box after a pen and comes out with a bottle of white liquid shoe polish, the dauber kind. “La Vang youth group car wash,” Kevin says. “We did windows.” “Y’all did windows,” Lena says, uncapping it, “and now I do this one.” On the back glass, in big white capitals that run a little at the bottoms: WHO DAT · 8 DAYS. She steps back to admire it. “Cut-down day. They get it to fifty-three by this afternoon. Nothing counts till Detroit.” “That’s my mom’s window,” Kevin says. “Your mama is a Catholic, Kevin. She’ll understand.”

Then she turns over a St. Brendan’s bulletin from last Sunday and does the gas on the back of it, out loud, at state-final speed. “Three hundred and ten miles there and back. Kevin says nineteen to the gallon, and Kevin does not lie about mileage. Two ninety-nine at the Chevron. Forty-eight seventy-eight. Five ways — me, Laney, Margot, Kevin, you — nine seventy-six each, Youngstown.” From the SL, Theo: “And me?” “The convertible runs on its own money.” She caps the pen. “I don’t do math on sin.”

Nine seventy-six is a real piece of a week that started on the last of a St. Brigid’s envelope. But Jack has two shifts of tip share in his wallet, and it’s his. “I’ve got it,” he says. “I wash dishes at the Anchor now. Tuesdays, Thursdays, and starting next week, Saturdays.”
Lena looks up from the bulletin. “The *Anchor*.” Her eyes go narrow and bright. “Where you insulted the marionberry.” Then she goes back to her arithmetic.

body.text: He pays first, before Margot has her wallet out of the tote: a ten, a one and a quarter. “Nine seventy-six. And bus fare.”
body.else: He pays when it comes around to him: a ten, a one and a quarter. “Nine seventy-six. And bus fare.”

body.else: “From last Sunday,” he adds. “With my compliments.”

body: She accepts it like a treaty. Then she digs a Ziploc of change out of the tote — she would have a Ziploc of change — and counts two dimes and four pennies into his palm, one at a time, so he can watch her be fair. While she counts, he puts her number into the RAZR off the back of Kevin’s card. T9 gets LENA right on the first try, which feels like an omen.

choices.text: Ride with Theo in the SL.
response: Lena, already climbing into the van’s middle row with the Greek grammar: “Go on. Somebody has to keep him under ninety.” Theo revs the engine once, purely for her.

choices.text: Ride in the Odyssey with everybody.
response: Theo takes it without a flicker, sunglasses down, the engine catching. “Abandoner,” he calls over the harpsichord. “I’ll see you at the soup.”

s02a.slug: SATURDAY · 9:38 AM · US-101 SOUTH, LOS ALAMOS
body: By Los Alamos the fog has burned off and the country has gone gold: hills the color of a lion’s back, oaks scattered over them dark as dropped ink, vineyards combed into rows. The SL’s oxblood leather is cracked and warm under Jack’s legs. Theo drives well and fast and without ever seeming to try, one wrist hung over the top of the wheel, his grandfather’s Rolex throwing sun. Back at the on-ramp he let the Odyssey pass just so he could read the back window, and now it rides a hundred yards ahead of them at exactly sixty-five: WHO DAT · 8 DAYS, in a hand that writes like it’s arguing.

body.text: Tell Theo the van is winning. Kevin signals for curves. Laney wants to know if y’all can see the windmill yet. —L.

body: For a while neither of them talks; the wind does it for them. Then Theo says, to the windshield, “He’ll come by tomorrow. My father.” A mile of oaks. “He stays everywhere six minutes. My birthday. My graduation. The Oscars, I’m told.” He glances over, smiling like a host. “Time him.”

The iPhone in his lap buzzes. Theo thumbs it to speaker and leaves it face-up on his thigh; California’s hands-free law is a year old, and Theo treats it as advisory. “Darling,” says a woman’s voice, bright and trained, over the sound of small dogs having opinions. “Are you driving? You sound like you’re driving.” “I’m driving, Mom. You’re on speaker. I have a Catholic in the car.”

Theo’s mother is calling from the Peninsula, and she delivers the news the way some people give toasts. The dogs are fine. The dogs are traumatized. The Hockney is fine; it has been riding shotgun with the Pomeranian for a week and the two of them have bonded. The evacuation orders are lifting. She’ll be home tomorrow. “The sky over La Cañada is the color of a Creamsicle,” she says. “Everyone’s saying it now. I said it first.” Then, with interest: “Is that Theo’s Catholic? Hello, Theo’s Catholic.”

“Hello, Mrs. Vance.” “Oh, God — *Caroline*. Mrs. Vance lives in Malibu now, and she’s thirty-one.” She doesn’t sound angry about it; she sounds like a woman describing a restaurant she’s stopped going to. “Theo says you pray. Pray for my house, would you? You people are good at houses.” “St. Joseph does houses,” Jack says. “I’ll put in a word.” “I’ll take anyone,” Caroline says. “I’m not proud. I’m from Pasadena.”

A tone cuts in under her: call waiting. Theo looks at the screen and drops his mother mid-sentence — “Mom, it’s Pops, love you, bye” — and answers, and his voice goes where Jack heard it go once before, at the window in 412 on move-in day while the mountains behind his mother’s house burned: lower, younger, careful, all the polish sanded off. “Hey. Hey, Pops. No, I’m driving. The car. Yes, *that* car.” He listens. “Did you skip it, or did they cancel it?” He listens longer. Ahead of them the Odyssey’s brake lights flick on for a curve and off again. “Pops. The mountains were on fire. That counts as a reason.” A pause. “No. No, you’re not in trouble. I’ll ask him.”
He hangs up and turns the phone face-down and drives for a while. “My sister,” he says at last. “Poppy. She’s fourteen.”

journal.title: Poppy
journal.text: Theo’s sister. Fourteen. He always picks up.

choices.text: “Tell me about Poppy.”
response: Theo takes a long time, for Theo, which is most of a vineyard. “She’s the only person in my family who calls to ask how I am,” he says, “and then waits for the answer.” He just drives.

choices.text: “You have a phone voice. It’s adorable.”
response: “Nobody will believe you.” A mile later, on purpose, in the voice: “Hey, Pops.” Then he slides Jack a look over the sunglasses that dares him to say one more word about it, and Jack, wisely, says nothing until Buellton.

choices.text: Say nothing. Watch the hills.
response: Jack watches the hills go by, gold and oak and gold. After a mile Theo says, to the road and not to him, “Thank you.”

s02b.slug: SATURDAY · 9:38 AM · US-101 SOUTH, THE ODYSSEY
body: South of Los Alamos the 101 runs through oak country gone blond for the summer, vineyards combed up the hills, the sky come in hard and blue. Kevin drives his mother’s Odyssey at exactly sixty-five, hands at ten and two. The van smells of Tiger Balm and Hawaiian Aloha Febreze, and the La Vang rosary on the mirror swings out on every curve and clicks against the windshield coming back. Somewhere up ahead, Theo is doing whatever Theo does to a speed limit.
Margot rides shotgun. Laney has the back bench and two of her three suitcases. Jack and Lena have the middle captain’s chairs, with an aisle of gray carpet between them about the width of a missal.

body.text: Laney is in Jack’s gray Mooney hoodie, sleeves down past her fingertips, wearing it as if he’d only ever been keeping it warm for her.

Since Thursday’s lunch Kevin has treated Jack as his audience. At the Los Alamos exit he finds him in the rearview. “Costigan. What did the ocean say to the beach?” “Kevin.” “Nothing. It just *waved*.” Lena turns all the way around to give Kevin a look of deep pastoral concern, and Kevin, thrilled, does the wheeze he laughs with when he’s the only one laughing.
body.else: At the Los Alamos exit Kevin reads the itinerary card aloud, times included, and nobody has the heart to stop him.

body: Through the back window Lena’s shoe polish reads backwards against the road unspooling behind them — SYAD 8 · TAD OHW. She twists around every few miles to check on it, in case it’s been converted.

Then the station out of Santa Barbara puts on the piano — that piano, the one every American under forty was issued at birth — and the van sings whether it wants to or not. Laney sings like she’s auditioning. Kevin knows every word and delivers each one at precisely the speed limit. Lena takes *streetlight people* with the lungs of a girl raised on parade routes, slapping time on her armrest, and on *hold on to that feeling* she looks across the carpet at Jack, and it would be a sin not to sing.

Margot doesn’t sing and is somehow the loudest person in the van. “Note the collective effervescence,” she tells her Moleskine. “Durkheim. Five members of the aspiring professional class performing working-class longing in a vehicle with a DVD player. Also, south of Detroit is Canada.” “It is *not*,” says Kevin, who has seen *8 Mile*. Nobody checks a map. Everybody sings louder.

When Journey lets go of them, Laney declares a game: impressions, and nobody leaves the van till everybody’s done one. She does Sloane — chin tucked, eyes enormous, a hand landing light as a moth on an invisible forearm: “Tell me about your *philanthropy*.” Kevin does Priya without taking his eyes off the road: “Per my email.”

Then Lena does Hale, and it is devastating. She barely bothers with the accent; she does the boredom: slumps into her chair like a man sinking into a club armchair after a long lunch, lets an invisible roster drop from her fingertips, and addresses a point six inches above everyone’s head in a drawl like a man reading a wine list he finds disappointing. “Prove to me you have a soul. You have ninety minutes, and I’ve had *lunch*.” She was in Hollis 302 for the original. So was Jack. Hers is better. Kevin drifts onto the rumble strip and back.

Margot, without turning around, does Lena in PHIL 1: the index finger up, the vowels a half step too warm and a whole step too fast. “Aquinas, *Summa*, first part, question six — *neither horn*.” Lena gasps as if struck with a glove. “Oh, Magdalena is *going* to say something. I do *not* sound like that.” “You sound exactly like that,” says the van. Lena is outraged. Lena is delighted. “I am going to *get* you, Lindqvist,” she tells the back of Margot’s head, radiant.
Then the van turns to Jack.

choices.text: Do Hale: the spaniel.
response: Jack lets his chin sink, finds a drawl soaked in contempt, and gives them Hale on the first day: *a girl who left as though I’d set fire to her coffee, and a boy who went after her like a spaniel*. Lena laughs with her head thrown back against the seat, and then, because she has never once left a thing alone, she does it better. “More contempt, Costigan. He says *spaniel* like it’s a diagnosis.” She does it again. It is worse. It is about him. He can’t stop grinning.

choices.text: Do Lena.
response: He pushes his sleeves up to the elbow. That’s all it takes; the van knows. The chin, the finger, the Lincoln-Douglas cadence, the sentence that builds and breaks on its last word: “*Cite* me.” The van dies. Lena stares at him with her mouth open, and then she retaliates. She pats her own back pocket for a paperback that isn’t there, uncaps an invisible red pen, and writes in the margin of an invisible paragraph, saying it as she writes it: “*Coward*.” Then, with a squint and the whole flat width of Ohio: “What a *jagoff*.” It’s so exact he feels it in his back teeth: she has been watching him closely enough to have it. She doesn’t do the eyebrow. Laney, from the back: “Y’all need a chaperone.” Kevin, eyes on the road: “I’m right here.”

choices.text: Do Frank: “Close your mouth. You’ll catch flies.”
response: He folds his arms, fixes his eyes on a horizon two thousand miles east of the windshield, and lets his face go as still as his father’s in the cab of the Silverado. “Close your mouth. You’ll catch flies.” Nobody in this van has met Frank Costigan; they laugh anyway, because it’s plainly true. Lena only smiles at him across the carpet, quietly pleased, as if he’s shown her something out of his wallet. “Your daddy sounds like mine with the volume turned down.”

s03.slug: SATURDAY · 10:04 AM · PEA SOUP ANDERSEN’S, BUELLTON
body: At four minutes past ten a windmill rises out of the flats beside the Buellton exit, white sails turning slowly over a parking lot full of RVs. On the big sign two cartoon chefs in toques — Hap-Pea and Pea-Wee, according to the placemats — are splitting a single pea with a mallet and a chisel, which is either the joke of the whole enterprise or its theology.

body.text: The SL got there first, Theo taking the exit at seventy, and by the time the Odyssey noses into the lot he has a booth under a wall of blue Danish plates and is on his second bowl.
body.else: The champagne SL is already in the lot, parked across two spaces at an angle that says its driver had somewhere to be, which was here. Inside, under a wall of blue Danish plates, Theo has a booth and is on his second bowl.

body: Bottomless split pea, at ten in the morning. “Ironically,” Theo says, when Laney points this out. He has three bowls. Somewhere in the third the irony goes out of it, and he is simply a beautiful man eating soup with his eyes closed. Laney buys a souvenir spoon with a tiny windmill on the handle “for my hope chest.” Kevin reads the history of the restaurant off the back of the menu to anyone who’ll listen, which turns out to be Margot, who is taking notes on the Danes.

At the gift-shop register, between a pyramid of pea-soup cans and a rack of wooden clogs nobody has ever bought, Lena buys a red-and-white tin of peppermint Altoids. Jack doesn’t understand why until she turns to Kevin and says, “Hand.” Kevin holds out his palm. She pours the whole tin into it. Kevin looks down at a small white heap of mints. “Is this —” “Don’t you *dare*.” Kevin closes his fist over the mints and asks nothing further.

Then she reaches into her cardigan pocket and comes out with last Saturday’s cigarette. It has been riding in the oatmeal wool for a week — through a fire alarm, a seminar, a rush, a beach — and it shows: bent, flattened, gone soft at the filter. She lays it in the empty tin on its bed of white paper, gently, like a priest setting a relic into an altar stone. She borrows the cashier’s Sharpie and prints on the lid, in the courtroom capitals she uses in his margins when she means it most, RELIQUARY. Then she tears a strip off the register tape, writes on it in her small slanted hand, and folds it into the lid.

body.text: She snaps the lid shut and points the tin at him. “And you tried to hand me the whole pack like a *coward*.”
Theo watches the whole thing from the end of the counter, soup bowl in both hands, like a man at a premiere who has money in the picture.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse, 8/29. She’s keeping count.

choices.text: “First-, second-, third-class relics. What class is a Marlboro?”
response: She doesn’t look up from the lid. “Fourth. I’m founding it.” She blows on the Sharpie to dry it, which does nothing for Sharpie, and which she knows, and which she does anyway, because it is a ceremony and ceremonies have steps.

choices.text: “Technically, that’s my property.”
response: “You abandoned it at the scene.” She says it with perfect serenity and closes the lid on him. Jack hears Rafi’s abuela in it, and her week’s difference, and keeps that to himself, because she’s already winning and he doesn’t want to arm her.

choices.text: “Okay. Keep count.”
response: “Oh, I intend to.” The lid snaps. The tin goes into the cardigan pocket where one cigarette used to ride alone, and for the rest of the weekend Jack hears it when she walks: a small dry tick against her hip, like a rosary in a coat.

s04.slug: SATURDAY · 2:20 PM · BROAD BEACH, MALIBU · THE VANCE HOUSE
body: Past Buellton the 101 climbs to the Gaviota Pass and comes down through the gorge onto the whole Pacific at once, blue to the end of the world, oil platforms standing offshore in the haze. After that it’s three-plus hours of Labor Day: Santa Barbara at a crawl, Ventura in brake lights, the PCH past Point Mugu with every car in Los Angeles County going the same way.

body.text: Jack arrives with a sunburn on the arm he kept on the door and Theo humming something that isn’t a song.
body.else: Somewhere past Carpinteria Laney falls asleep on Margot’s shoulder, and Margot permits it, upright and unblinking, “as fieldwork.”

body: Brian Rolle, canonized by acclamation in a garage on Glenwood Avenue. Jack can hear Frank at the final gun, saying *Well* to the radio.

The house is glass and teak set down on the sand at Broad Beach, west of Zuma, below the highway, so that from the PCH all anybody sees is a gate and a garage and a hedge somebody trims with a ruler. Inside, it’s all window. Theo slides the glass doors open and the iPod dock picks up Animal Collective, a song like a heat wave remembered by someone happy. The air smells of salt and, faintly, of somebody else’s campfire. Every surface on the deck wears a fine gray film, soft as talc. Laney reaches for a chaise.

“Don’t touch the deck chairs,” Theo says. “That’s the mountains.” The fire is thirty-odd miles east, about half contained, the radio said at Oxnard. Out here the fire comes down as ash, settling on everything a man paid for. Kevin rubs a pinch of it between finger and thumb and says, “Particulate,” in the voice of a person who would like everyone to go inside.
Jack opens the refrigerator for a water, looks at what’s in it, and closes it again. He drinks from the tap.

The Oscar is in the downstairs powder room, on a glass shelf beside the folded hand towels, gold and heavier-looking than anything that size has a right to be. Jack is standing in front of it with his hands in his pockets when Kevin leans into the doorway beside him and reads the plaque and says, pleasantly, “So it was rehab or love.” Theo, passing down the hall with Laney’s second suitcase, doesn’t break stride. “Next question.” Kevin laughs. Theo doesn’t.

Lena and Laney get the ocean suite, which has a bathtub you could raise a family in. “Or start one,” says Laney, and Lena hits her with a pillow. Margot asks for “the room with no mirrors,” and Theo, after real thought, has one. Kevin takes the far end of the hall, near the exits. Jack is in Theo’s room, which looks like it’s been Theo’s since he was fifteen: *Point Break* on one wall and *The Third Man* on the other, a shelf of Criterion spines in strict alphabetical order, and under the window a twin bed made up for a guest. Laney is in the pool inside four minutes, shrieking about the temperature, which is heated.

Lena goes straight down the beach stairs in her Keds and into the Pacific to the ankle without taking them off, with the confidence of a woman raised on warm water, and stops dead. “Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian.” She turns around in the foam to face him, betrayed. “The Gulf is a *bath*. This is a *threat*.”

body.text: She lifts one dripping Ked out of the water and points it up the stairs at him. “The boots are resting,” she says. “My taste is on vacation.”

choices.text: Follow Lena down to the water.
response: Ankle-deep beside her, he gets her complaint against the Pacific in full: it’s cold, it’s loud, it has no manners, there are seals in it with the eyes of men who owe her money, and it does not have the decency to smell like anything but itself. She makes him put a bare foot in. He flinches; she crows so hard she has to hang on to his sleeve to stay upright in the backwash, and lets go as soon as the backwash does.

choices.text: Cannonball contest with Laney.
response: Laney judges from the water like it’s Miss Teen Dallas County. “Poise, two. Entry, a crime. Splash, a *ten*.” Margot scores from a chaise she has wiped first, holding up fingers without looking up from Ehrenreich, harsher by an average of three points and refusing to explain her rubric.

choices.text: Help Theo open up the house.
response: Shutters, breakers, the pool cover. At the end of a hall Theo opens a door on a screening room nobody uses — forty velvet seats in tiers, a screen like a wall, a popcorn machine still wrapped in plastic. “He built it for premiere parties,” Theo says, and stands in the doorway without going in. “He watches everything on a laptop in bed.”

s05.slug: SATURDAY · 5:30 PM · POINT DUME, THEN THE VANCE HOUSE KITCHEN
body: At half past five Lena opens Theo’s father’s refrigerator: steel, taller than Jack, lit like a museum case, and stacked with a chef’s plastic containers, each labeled in the same black marker: *R.V. — MON — DO NOT*. She reads one. She reads another. She shuts the door with her hip.

“Nobody eats a stranger’s labeled food in my presence,” she announces to the kitchen. “That’s a sin against hospitality. I’m cooking.” From the white couch, without lifting his head, Theo lobs the SL keys across the room. They hit Jack in the sternum. “Don’t kill the car.”

So Jack Costigan of Glenwood Avenue drives a champagne-gold 1979 Mercedes convertible down the Pacific Coast Highway with Lena Broussard in the passenger seat, the top down, smoke haze turning the low sun the color of a peach. Her hair is everywhere — across her face, in her mouth, a honey-colored riot she holds down with both hands and loses anyway, laughing at it, laughing at him for driving like his father, at the speed limit, in a car built to be driven badly. He would drive her to Oregon. She tells him to turn left at the light. When he asks what they’re doing: “Making groceries, Costigan.” His look. “It’s what you call it when you’re from somewhere.”

The market at Point Dume employs a man whose only job is misting the lettuce. Lena goes up and down the aisles appalled and delighted by turns. Okra, $7.99 a pound: “In Louisiana you can’t *give* okra away. People leave it on your porch like a threat.” No andouille, so she weighs a link of chorizo in her palm. “This is going to have to repent.” At the seafood case she reads the card on the shrimp — *farm-raised, product of Thailand* — and lays her hand flat on the glass. “My daddy sells Gulf shrimp for a living. Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. I’m going to call him and tell him about this, and he is going to *cry*.” She buys two pounds anyway, with chicken thighs and the vegetables and rice, and apologizes to the shrimp under her breath. From the bottom of the OCTAVIA tote she produces a can of Tony Chachere’s. “For somebody who wasn’t coming,” Jack says, “you packed Tony Chachere’s.” “A Catholic packs for the possibility of grace.”

body.text: Jack peels off for the pie he owes Theo: four peaches that smell like August, butter, flour. He pays for those himself, tip money from the Anchor jar, folded the way Gloria folds it. “A debt you pay with somebody else’s peaches isn’t paid.” “You can’t bake.” “I can wash a pie.” She regards him with pity and something like respect. “My mama’s crust. You’ll cut the butter in with two knives, because there is no pastry cutter in a house with an *Oscar*.”
body.else: Jack drifts toward the peaches, because somebody ought to make a pie and it might as well be a man who never has: four that smell like August, butter, flour, paid for with tip money from the Anchor jar. “You can’t bake.” “I can wash a pie.” She regards him with pity and something like respect. “My mama’s crust. You’ll cut the butter in with two knives, because there is no pastry cutter in a house with an *Oscar*.”

body: Everything else she pays for, moving him out of the way with a hand flat on his chest. “My kitchen, my tab.”

Back at the house she plugs her iPod into the speakers in the ceiling, and the Meters come down out of the plaster: a drum break, a bassline in no hurry, a guitar that’s been up since Thursday. Lena ties her hair back with a rubber band from the junk drawer and drapes her cardigan over a stool, and her Ked squeaks on the tile where the Pacific got into it this afternoon.

Crust first. He cuts cold butter into flour with two steak knives from a drawer full of them while she corrects his technique without touching him, miming it in the air an inch above his knuckles. “Smaller. Peas, not dice.” Ice water by the spoonful. They find a porcelain pie dish with the price sticker still on it, and he lays in the crust and the peaches and the lid, crimps the edge with his thumb as she shows him, and slides it into the oven feeling absurdly like a father.
Then the roux. Oil and flour in the heaviest pot in the house, a medium flame, and she puts a wooden spoon in his hand and holds on to the other end of it a moment.

“A roux is a vow, Costigan. Flour and fat and forty-five minutes. You don’t stop stirring, you don’t walk away. Peanut butter, then a penny, then a Hershey bar. You burn it, you start over and you tell nobody.”

body.text: She lets go of the spoon. “You handed me a flask like a gentleman Friday. I’m handing you a spoon. Don’t make me regret it.”

body: Jack has renewed his baptismal promises in front of a bishop. Nobody handed him a spoon. He stirs.

She does the onions, celery and pepper beside him, the knife going fast. “The holy trinity. Make one joke about Sabellius and I’ll put you in the pot.” While she chops, she diagnoses the refrigerator. Gluttony, per Gregory the Great by way of Aquinas, has five ways — she rattles off the Latin like a jump-rope rhyme, *praepropere, laute, nimis, ardenter, studiose*: too soon, too expensively, too much, too eagerly, too daintily. She points the knife at the steel door. “*Laute* and *studiose*. Expensive and fussy. It’s a confessional with a freezer.” Theo, passing through with an orange: “Take the wine with the ugliest label. It’s the expensive one.” She does. A splash goes in the pot later; one glass sits at her elbow, and she drinks it slowly.

Somewhere around peanut butter Jack sees it: a streak of flour high on her left cheekbone, left over from the crust, bright as chalk on the gold of her skin. He can’t take his hand off the spoon, so he points at his own face with his chin. She wipes the right cheek. Wrong one. She lifts her eyebrows: better? It is not better. The easy thing would be to reach over with his thumb. He knows the distance, about the length of his forearm, and what her cheek would feel like at the end of it. He keeps his hand on the spoon. The roux goes from peanut butter toward copper, and he keeps his eyes on it.

She bends to check the pie through the oven door, meets herself in the black glass, and finds the flour. She wipes it off with the back of her wrist. She doesn’t turn around. “Okay, *fine*,” she says, dry, to the oven. His own red ink, returned with interest.

At 8:04 by the stove clock the LG goes off in the cardigan on the stool, and she lights up — there is no other word for it — wipes her hands down her dress, and is out the glass door to the deck with the phone at her ear. Eight-oh-four on the dot. Over her shoulder: “Don’t you *dare* stop.”

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Called at 8:04 on the dot.

choices.text: Keep stirring. Don’t look.
response: He keeps stirring and doesn’t look at the glass. Copper, then darker, the smell going nutty and deep, the spoon dragging figure eights across the bottom of the pot. At 8:19 she comes back in with the phone folded in her hand and leans over the stove. The roux is the color of a Hershey bar.
“Well,” she says. “Look at you.” No joke attached, nothing to hide behind: plain admiration, handed over straight, and he has to look at the pot to take it.

choices.text: Stir, and listen to her laugh through the glass.
response: He stirs and lets himself listen. Through the glass he can’t make out a word, only her laugh, coming and going under the surf. It’s 8:04; it’s Wes. Whatever he’s saying, he’s making her laugh, and making her laugh well. Jack is glad. He is honestly glad, and it isn’t free, and he keeps stirring, and the two facts ride along side by side in him like strangers on a bus.
At 8:19 she comes back and looks in the pot. “Milk chocolate with ambition.”

choices.text: Turn the Meters up and make the stirring a show for Laney’s BlackBerry.
response: He cranks the Meters. Laney has the pink BlackBerry up inside a second — “Y’all. He’s *stirring*” — and Jack stirs like he’s conducting the Cleveland Orchestra, free arm swooping on the upbeat, spoon never once leaving the pot. Kevin dances with a dish towel. Margot times it on the Nokia. “Minute nine. The subject continues to perform domestic labor for a female audience.” Laney turns the screen around: she’s already posted about it.

response.name: Laney Price
response.text: is in MALIBU watching a Catholic stir a roux for Jesus. 9 minutes and counting. he has not looked up ONCE
response.meta: Saturday at 8:13pm via Facebook for BlackBerry · Theo Vance likes this

response: The roux survives. At 8:19 Lena comes back, looks in the pot, looks at Laney’s screen, looks at Jack. “Milk chocolate. Acceptable. Barely.”

s06.slug: SATURDAY · 9:40 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE DECK
body: The gumbo takes an hour, and then it takes the deck. By twenty to ten they’re all out at the long teak table — Kevin hosed the ash off the chairs at sundown, without being asked — with citronella going in hurricane glasses, the surf heavy and invisible under the boards, and the glass house lit up behind them. Six bowls of gumbo over rice, dark as strong coffee and smelling like a kitchen in a city Jack has never seen.

Lena stands for grace, because she was raised in a house where whoever cooked says it. “Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord.” Jack and Kevin say the Amen with her and cross themselves at the same speed, parish-school speed. Laney bows so extravagantly a strand of copper lands in her bowl. Margot does not bow. Margot eats two bowls. “Colonial,” she pronounces, at the bottom of the second, “but correct.” Kevin estimates the protein aloud — “Shrimp, chicken, the chorizo, that’s like fifty grams, Lena, that’s a recovery meal” — and Theo eats slowly and offers no opinions, which from Theo is a rave.

Through the glass, on a television about as wide as a pool table, LSU is playing Washington on ESPN with the sound off: two teams that both chose purple and gold, under the lights in Seattle. Lena has turned her chair to keep it in view. Her LG lights every few minutes, and she reads the texts aloud, capitals intact, at volume. “Remy. My brother. He’s at LSU, which is a decision he makes again every morning.” She turns the phone around so the table can see.

body.text: TOLIVER!!!!
TELL YOUR CALIFORNIA PEOPLE GEAUX TIGERS

body: “Tell him the California people say *geaux*,” says Laney. “I’m not his people,” says Margot. Lena thumbs out a reply in complete sentences with punctuation, which takes long enough that Washington scores.

body.text: Then Jack goes inside and comes back with the pie. The crust has browned to the color of a church pew and the peaches have bubbled up through the vents and burned a little at the edges, and Lena leans over to inspect her mother’s crust in a stranger’s dish and declares it “not a disgrace,” which in her family is a medal. He sets it down in front of Theo with a knife beside it. Theo looks at the pie for a while. “People owe me,” he says. “Nobody pays.” Then he picks up the knife and cuts into it, and without looking up from the cutting: “Does He take IOUs? Your God. Or is it cash on delivery?”

body: Down the table Lena has gone still with her fork halfway, the way she does in seminar when somebody says the interesting thing by accident. The question is not for her. She leaves it on the table where Theo put it.

journal.text: Paid Theo one peach pie, Lena’s mother’s crust. Marionberry still 4/10.

choices.text: “He’s the one who pays. That’s the whole scandal.”
choices.key: You told Theo God is the one who pays.
response: Theo looks at him across the citronella. “Huh.” He cuts a second slice and puts it on his plate beside the first and doesn’t eat it. He just sits with it, the knife across the plate, while under the deck the tide works at the pilings.

choices.text: “Depends what’s on the IOU.”
response: Theo turns the knife over in his hand. “Hypothetically?” He considers the blade. “A lot.” Then Kevin comes out through the glass with a stack of plates and a carton of Häagen-Dazs he found behind the R.V. containers, unlabeled, which Lena says is fair game, and the subject goes back wherever Theo keeps it.

choices.text: “Cash only. He’s been known to accept pie.”
response: Theo takes the joke and the biggest slice. “Then I’m covered through Lent.” He eats it with his fingers, crust and all, and holds out his plate for more before anybody else has been served, which is as close as Theo comes to saying a thing was good.

s06b.slug: SATURDAY · 11:50 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE DEN
body: The den has a couch as long as a lifeboat, a rug with camels on it, and an Xbox 360 with a plastic drum kit, two plastic guitars and a plastic microphone.

body.text: “He bought it for Poppy,” Theo says, from the couch. “She’s played it once.”
body.else: “He bought it for my sister,” Theo says, from the couch. “Poppy. She’s fourteen. She’s played it once.”

body: Lena takes the drums. She puts her hair up with a pencil stabbed through it, sets one Ked on the kick pedal, and plays Bon Jovi on Hard like Bon Jovi has wronged her family. Margot takes the bass and stands perfectly motionless while her fingers work. “I’m performing alienation.” Kevin sings it — every note, the key change, the impossible top of the chorus — perfectly, and apologizes between verses. Laney is the crowd; she stands on the couch and screams at the right moments and several wrong ones. Theo stays where he is, an arm along the back of the couch, and watches, and doesn’t play.

Jack takes guitar on Easy and fails out twice. Both times his lane goes gray and the digital crowd boos, and both times Lena hits a fill and brings him back from the dead with Overdrive, which in Rock Band is a thing the drummer can do. The second time she doesn’t even look over. “That’s two, Youngstown. I’m keeping count.”

Between songs her phone lights on the arm of the couch. She reads it standing on the drum throne, stick raised: “Thirty-one twenty-three, TIGERS.” At half past twelve Margot hands the bass to Theo, who lays it on the rug without playing a note, and goes off to the room with no mirrors with a book and no evident plan to sleep. Theo dangles the SL keys at Jack from the couch. “The PCH is empty at this hour. You drive. Ninety to Zuma and back, top down. Your Broussard will never know.” Jack shakes his head. Theo pockets the keys, unoffended, as if he’s only checking that the offer still works.

At one o’clock Jack goes to the den window for air. Below, the pool is lit from underneath, a long blue room in the dark. Kevin sits at one end with his feet in the water. Theo sits at the other end with his. Neither of them is talking. After a while Kevin takes his feet out, picks up his sandals, and goes inside.

body.text: When Jack turns around, Laney is asleep on the chaise by the glass doors in the Mooney hoodie, her BlackBerry face-down on her chest, rising and falling.
body.else: When Jack turns around, Laney is asleep on the chaise by the glass doors, her BlackBerry face-down on her chest, rising and falling.

body: Lena finds a striped beach towel in the basket by the door, and they lay it over her together, Jack at the feet, Lena tucking it under Laney’s chin. “She’ll say she wasn’t asleep.” She pulls the pencil out of her hair and the hair comes down, and she stands a second in the blue light off the pool with a drumstick still in her other hand. “Goodnight, Youngstown.” She goes off down the hall toward the ocean suite, the tin ticking in her cardigan pocket, until a door closes at the end of it.
Jack shuts off the Xbox. The plastic drum pads are scuffed white where she hit them. Under the towel Laney says, very clearly, “I’m not asleep,” and is.

s07.slug: SUNDAY · 5:50 AM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE DECK
body: The quiet wakes him. No sea lions barking off the wharf, no gulls clattering on Delgado’s roof, no freight horn — only the surf under the deck, soft and enormous, breathing. Across Theo’s room, Theo’s bed is empty. Jack pulls on the Carhartt and goes out. The light is gray, and the marine layer lies on the sand, thick and low.

Margot is on the deck already, on a chair she has wiped clean with a dish towel — the towel, black with ash, is folded on the rail — with her thermos and her Moleskine and her black cardigan buttoned to the throat. She has not slept. She looks exactly the way she looks when she has. Past the corner of the house, where the side path runs up to the drive, the place where the SL was parked is an empty square of concrete.

“Your roommate’s car left at two-forty,” Margot says. “He doesn’t sleep.” “Neither do I. That’s how I know.” She unscrews the thermos cap, fills it, and hands it to him without asking whether he wants it. It is very strong and very bad, and he drinks all of it.

His paperback is where he left it on the next chair: Evelyn Waugh, *Brideshead Revisited*, the Back Bay edition, three dollars off the sidewalk cart at Driftwood, spine already cracked white by somebody before him. The Benedict holy card has migrated from *Spe Salvi* to mark his place. Margot regards it. “You know what that book is about.” “Grace.” “Men in love with each other in a very large house.” Jack turns the book over in his hands. “It can be about two things.” “Everything is,” Margot says, and drinks from the thermos itself.

For a while they sit with the ocean. Then, to the water, in a register close to true: “Every house like this has a room nobody uses. In ours it was my parents’ marriage.” She doesn’t look over to see what he does with that, and he doesn’t do anything with it, which seems to be the right thing; she uncaps a pen.

The Moleskine falls open on her knee to a fresh page. She writes the date at the top, and then looks up at his left eyebrow with the steady, unembarrassed interest she brings to everything. “The eyebrow,” she says. “For the file.”

choices.text: “Sister Mary Clement. Third grade. A ruler. She was aiming for my soul.”
response: She writes it down verbatim, then adds a line beneath it: *Catholic school: corporal punishment. Predictable.* She underlines *Predictable* twice and turns the notebook so he can see that she has.
choices.key: You told Margot a nun gave you the scar.

choices.text: “A jealous husband. Erie, Pennsylvania.”
response: “You’re eighteen.” “I was younger.” Margot looks at him over the black frames, unblinking, for the length of a set. “That’s the worst lie anyone has ever told me,” she says, “and my father is a sociologist.”
choices.key: You told Margot a jealous husband gave you the scar.

choices.text: “Not for the file.”
response: She looks at him for a while. Then she closes the Moleskine and puts the pen in the spiral. “Then it stays out of the Moleskine.” She doesn’t ask again, and she doesn’t write anything else down, and it’s the first time he has seen her decide not to.
choices.key: You kept the scar out of Margot’s file.

s08.slug: SUNDAY · 9:00 AM · OUR LADY OF MALIBU
body: Kevin drives, because it’s his mother’s van and because nobody else was asked. The Odyssey goes down the PCH at the speed limit with the windows down and the 7 DAYS on the back glass still tacky. Lena has the captain’s chair across the aisle from Jack, in the green dress with sleeves she calls her church one and the white Keds, her black lace mantilla folded on her knee. Margot is finally asleep.

body.text: Laney has the back bench to herself, in Jack’s Mooney hoodie over a yellow sundress, sunglasses on, sitting very straight with her hands folded in her lap like a girl waiting to be called up at a recital. “I’ve never been to a Catholic one,” she announces. “Is it like a wedding without the bar?”
body.else: Laney has the back bench to herself, in a yellow sundress and a cardigan buttoned to the neck, sunglasses on, sitting very straight with her hands folded in her lap like a girl waiting to be called up at a recital. “I’ve never been to a Catholic one,” she announces. “Is it like a wedding without the bar?”

body: “It’s exactly like a wedding, cher,” Lena says. “Same groom every week.” Kevin finds her in the rearview. “Theologically sound.” “I know it is, Kevin. I’m from New Orleans. We don’t joke about the groom.”

Our Lady of Malibu is cool inside after the glare and smells of beeswax and good sunscreen. The congregation is in linen: linen shirts, linen trousers, a linen sundress on a woman with a linen baby. A man in the pew ahead has a sweater knotted over his shoulders in September in Malibu, which seems to Jack an act of faith in its own right. Lena shakes out the mantilla and puts it on without ceremony, and two linen heads turn, and she lets them. The celebrant, the bulletin says, is a priest on supply for the month, Irish, sunburned along the part in his hair. *The Lord be with you. And also with you.*
Lena runs Laney through the Mass in whispers, her mouth an inch from Laney’s ear. Stand. Sit. Stand. During the Gloria she slides the bulletin into Laney’s lap. She has written on the back of it.

body.title: Back of the Our Lady of Malibu bulletin, Lena’s hand
body.text:
STAND when he stands.
SIT for the readings.
KNEEL at the bells.
At Communion: ARMS CROSSED. You’ll get a blessing.
Do NOT take the cup.
You are doing beautifully. —L.

body: The first reading is Isaiah, the ears of the deaf cleared, the lame leaping like a stag. Then a lector in a seersucker jacket gets up and reads James to a church full of gold rings. *For if a man with gold rings and fine clothes comes into your assembly, and a poor person in shabby clothes also comes in, and you say to the one in fine clothes, Sit here, please, while you say to the poor one, Stand there —* Lena’s eyebrow goes up and stays up. Jack studies his shoes, which are the only shoes in the building that came from a Payless. Kevin, at the end of the pew, very carefully does not look at anyone. The man with the sweater turns his wedding ring around his finger once, all the way, and leaves it.

The Gospel is Mark, the deaf man brought to Jesus, and Jesus taking him off by himself, away from the crowd. He puts his finger into the man’s ears. He says *Ephphatha* — be opened — and Lena’s lips make the Aramaic along with the priest, soundlessly, as if mouthing a song she loves. The homily is short. The priest comes down one step and says only this, in a brogue: “He puts his fingers in the man’s ears. He doesn’t shout at him from across the road.” Then he sits down, and the church sits there with it.

At the bells Laney braces her Tory Burch flats on the padded rail, and Lena puts a hand on her knee and leans in: “That’s a kneeler, cher, not a footrest.” Laney kneels, wobbling, and looks around to see if she’s doing it right. She is; Lena’s nod says so. At Communion Lena leans over once more, close, the mantilla brushing Laney’s copper hair. “Cross your arms over your chest and he’ll bless you.” Laney crosses them experimentally. “Like a vampire?” “Like a *Baptist*.” Laney goes up the aisle between Lena and Jack, arms crossed, chin up, and the Irish priest lays his hand on her copper head and says something to her nobody else can hear. She comes back down the side aisle pink to the hairline and very quiet, and kneels when Lena kneels, and stays down a while after Lena has sat back.

At five past ten they come out into the glare and the SL is at the curb. Fog has run down the windshield in the night; the wipers have drawn two clean fans through it, and there’s a fine film of dried salt everywhere the wipers didn’t reach. Theo is leaning against the champagne door in sunglasses and yesterday’s jeans, holding a cardboard tray with four coffees in it.

“I don’t go in,” he says, before anyone has said anything. “I’m a supporter, not a member.” He hands out the coffees, black for Jack, something with foam for Laney, a cortado for Lena that she didn’t order and is correct, Kevin’s with a sleeve on it. Laney holds her cup in both hands. “Theodore. I got *blessed*.” Theo looks at her over the sunglasses. “I can see that. You’re luminous. It’s upsetting.”

Jack walks down the steps with his coffee to where the one bar lives on the RAZR. The note his mother tucked in with the envelope from St. Brigid’s is still in his wallet: *call Nonna Sunday after Mass.* It’s after one o’clock on Glenwood Avenue. The extension in Nonna’s room picks up on the fourth ring, fumbles, and EWTN comes on behind her like a radiator. “Giacomino.” He asks for his mother. “Your mother is with your brother,” Nonna says, which is all she says about that, and Jack says “Okay,” and looks at the ocean across the highway for a second, and doesn’t ask anything else.

body.text: Then, darker: “Giacomino. Primo venerdì.” A pause he could drive the Silverado through. “You went?”
body.else: Then, darker: “You went to Mass today?” “I’m on the steps right now, Nonna.” “Bravo.” A pause he could drive the Silverado through. “And Friday? Primo venerdì. You went?”

choices.text: “No, Nonna. I played chess with the priest.”
choices.key: You told Nonna you played chess with the priest instead of going to confession.
response: “Chess!” Two thousand miles of static can’t hide what she does with her face; he can hear it. “*Madonna.*” Then, considering: “Did you win?” “No.” “Good,” says Nonna. “Go next week.” And she hangs up on herself, three tries to find the cradle, and he stands on the steps of a church in Malibu with the dial tone and the coffee and the distinct sense that he’s been given a penance by an eighty-four-year-old woman with a remote control.

choices.text: “I went to Mass Thursday.”
response: “Thursday is not Friday, Giacomino.” A sigh comes all the way from Glenwood Avenue, through Pennsylvania and the plains and the desert, and arrives intact. “October,” she says. “I write it on the calendar.” He can hear her doing it, the pen from the drawer by the bed, the calendar from the funeral home with the Sacred Heart on it. She hangs up before he can promise.

choices.text: “I went.”
response: “Bravo,” Nonna says, and she sounds so pleased. She tells him she lit a candle for it already, just in case, and now it counts double. Standing in the sun on the church steps with Theo’s coffee going cold in his hand, Jack wishes she didn’t sound pleased, and she says “Ciao, bello,” and finds the cradle on the first try.

s09.slug: SUNDAY · 11:15 AM · THE VANCE HOUSE, KITCHEN
body: Out the kitchen window the Odyssey’s back glass now reads 7 DAYS. Lena did it in the drive before Mass, in her church dress, with a wet thumb and the shoe polish, while Kevin stood by with a paper towel for his mother’s sake. On the counter Theo has laid out, from nowhere, three timed tickets to the Getty Villa, still warm from the house printer. “Meridian has a relationship with antiquities,” he says.

Margot takes one off the counter without asking. “Everyone’s father has a relationship with antiquities. My mother *is* one.” Lena turns. “Your mother — ” “Classics. Reed.” Lena looks at her as if Margot has just produced a second, secret head. Then she picks up the third ticket and holds it out across the island to Jack. “Youngstown. Herakles. Coming?”

Out the glass doors, the afternoon is already set: Laney on an inflatable swan in the pool with a mimosa, Theo’s iPhone ringing on a side table and Theo already reaching for it, and Kevin on the edge of a chaise with a bottle of sunscreen in one hand, looking at the mimosa.

choices.text: The Getty Villa with Lena and Margot.
choices.key: You spent Sunday afternoon at the Getty Villa with Lena.
response: Lena snags Kevin’s keys off the counter and jingles them. “I’m driving.” From out by the pool, Kevin, with feeling: “Please don’t.”

choices.text: Stay at the house with Theo, Laney and Kevin.
choices.key: You stayed at the house with Theo, Laney and Kevin.
response: Lena takes it in stride and the ticket back. “Your loss,” she says, tucking it into the tote. “Herakles is *ripped*.”

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Doesn’t sleep. Possibly my friend.

s09a.slug: SUNDAY · 12:40 PM · THE GETTY VILLA, PACIFIC PALISADES
body: Lena drives. She takes Kevin’s keys, Kevin’s mother’s Odyssey and the Pacific Coast Highway in that order, and merges onto the last of these without what Jack would call a look. “I’ve driven a seafood truck down Banks Street since I was fifteen,” she says, already in the fast lane. “With ice in the back. *Sloshing*.” The La Vang rosary swings out on the mirror and clicks home and swings out again. The van has never been so frightened. Margot rides the back bench with both oxblood boots braced against the seat in front of her, taking notes in a hand that gets worse at every light, while the shoe polish on the back glass informs the traffic of Los Angeles County that it is seven days to Detroit.

The Villa sits up a canyon above the highway: a Roman country house buried at Herculaneum and built again out of new stone by a man with the money to do it. You come in through the long garden — green water with nothing moving on it, bronzes along its edges, boxwood clipped square as a hymnal, and past the far wall the ocean, pewter in the smoke haze. It smells of bay laurel and hot stone and, faintly, of the mountains burning.

Lena goes through it like a girl let out of school early. She says *peristyle* like Laney says *Pi Lam*. Inside, in a cool gallery with a marble floor, she plants herself in front of a grave stele — a woman seated, a man standing, carved in low relief, their right hands clasped — and reads the Greek over their heads aloud for him at a gallop, her finger moving an inch from the stone: two names, and the word the Athenians gave their dead. *Chaire.* Farewell; rejoice; it means both. “They always shake hands,” she says. “The dead and the living. Half the time nobody can tell which one’s leaving.”

From behind them, without looking up from the Moleskine: “*Khaî*-re.” Margot gives the circumflex its whole shape, the pitch climbing and coming back down. “It rises and falls. You’re saying it like Erasmus. Erasmus was Dutch.” Lena turns around very slowly, the map pressed flat to her collarbone. “The restored pronunciation,” Margot says. “My mother would have you deported.” “You *wretch*,” Lena says, thrilled. “Again.” Margot says it again. Lena says it back. Margot shakes her head and says it a third time, slower, and Lena follows the pitch up and down like a girl learning a jump-rope rhyme, all the way across the gallery, until a docent turns around and Margot, with deep reluctance, gives her a nod. On her own ground, in a dead language, on a Sunday, somebody has beaten her, and she has studied the winner on the spot.

On the terrace Lena delivers the fact she has plainly been saving since Theo printed the tickets: J. Paul Getty paid for every stone of this place and died two years after it opened without once coming to see it. Margot considers the house. “A billionaire built a fake Roman house so he could own the real statues. It’s the most American object in California.” “And it’s *free*,” Lena says. “He never came, and everybody gets in.” Margot takes a while deciding whether to count that one for her.

The Herakles has a small round room to himself at the heart of the house, and stands in the middle of it in white marble a little bigger than life: young, beardless, a club over his left shoulder and the lion’s skin hanging from his right hand, his weight on one leg like a man waiting to be asked. The card says he was found in pieces near Hadrian’s villa in 1790 and put back together. Up close you can see the seams. In the galleries are the ones nobody put back: a torso gone at both shoulders, a goddess with no face below the eyes, a boy missing his nose since before Charlemagne.
Lena has a green composition book open against her forearm, the paper she owes him already half in it. She looks from the torso to the hero and back.

body.text: “You said bleed on yours,” she tells him, uncapping her pen. “I’m about to.”

body: “A broken statue is still Herakles.” Her pen is moving before she’s done saying it. “The damage is real and the form’s still there. That’s Gage. That’s my paper.”

In the garden on the way out there is a fountain set into a wall under a half-dome of mosaic: blue glass, shells, masks with their mouths open, sea creatures nobody has ever caught. Lena wants it close. She steps up onto the rim of the basin in her Keds to lecture the tiles about tesserae, and when he comes close to see she puts a hand on his shoulder and leans on it like a banister, and goes on lecturing from up there — smalti, cut glass, the Romans’ blue — with half her weight on his collarbone and no apology. When she’s finished with the Romans she uses the shoulder to come down by, lands on the gravel, and pats it twice, as if returning a library book. Across the garden, under a laurel, Margot clears her throat at a bronze.
Lena turns back to him, pen up, brisk as a nun with a clipboard, waiting for his red ink.

choices.text: “That’s your paper. That’s the answer to Gage.”
response: “I know.” She caps the pen. “I wanted to hear you say it.” She says it lightly. It doesn’t land lightly, and the two of them stand in the laurel smell a second with that, until Margot calls from the colonnade that it’s half past four and she has no intention of being locked in with anybody’s epiphany.

journal.title: Designated antagonists
journal.text: Two pages a week, bled on in red. Her next one: a broken statue is still Herakles. I’m going to need more pens.

choices.text: “A statue doesn’t feel the arm go.”
response: She stops on the gravel as if he’s taken something out of her hand. “Neither did Gage, after.” Then she turns the composition book sideways against her knee and writes his objection into her own paper, in her own hand, word for word, with his name after it in parentheses. He has seen what she does to sentences she doesn’t respect. This is the opposite, and it is the highest compliment she pays.

choices.text: “Twelve labors, and nobody could keep his nose on.”
response: She laughs out loud, in a museum, a laugh that goes up the colonnade and comes back down off the marble. A guard in a blue blazer turns around. Lena holds up a hand — *sorry, sorry* — and is visibly not sorry, and when she catches sight of the goddess with no face she goes again, helpless, holding on to a column.

s09b.slug: SUNDAY · 12:40 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE POOL
body: The van takes Lena and Margot off down the PCH, Kevin watching it go like a father at a school bus, and the afternoon settles. The pool is a blue rectangle laid along the deck above the beach stairs. The chaises are clean; Kevin hosed them again at half past eleven. Now he sits in the one patch of shade in a navy quarter-zip and SPF 50, in eighty-five degrees, reading an MCAT prep book as if for fun.

body.text: Laney drifts in the middle of the pool on the swan, Jack’s Mooney hoodie over a bikini, sleeves pushed to the elbows, a cardinal on a swan at noon in Malibu. She has balanced a champagne flute of mimosa in the crook of the swan’s neck.
body.else: Laney drifts in the middle of the pool on the swan in a bikini and very large sunglasses, a champagne flute of mimosa balanced in the crook of the swan’s neck.

body.text: Theo, flat on a chaise with his face to the sun, doesn’t open his eyes. “Careful, Costigan. They go for the eyebrow.” Laney paddles round. “Who does?” “Swans. He has a history.” Laney looks from the swan to Jack and lowers her sunglasses, thrilled. “Fireman. Did a *bird* do that?”

body: She paddles to the edge, folds her arms on the warm coping and sets the flute down beside her elbow. From the beach bag at the edge she fishes a small silver pillbox. Even from the chaise Jack can read the engraving: DRP. She shakes one small white pill into her palm, at noon, and chases it with the mimosa.

body.text: He has seen the box before, Friday night, on the sidewalk outside Pi Lam, under a different sky.

body: Kevin closes the MCAT book on his thumb. He gets up, goes to the outdoor kitchen, pours a glass of orange juice, walks over to the edge of the pool and picks up the champagne flute and sets the orange juice down in its place, all without a word, and goes back to the shade. Laney looks at the orange juice. She doesn’t look at Kevin. After a little while she picks it up and drinks it.

Then she pushes off and turns the swan with one hand so she can see the chaise. “Is your daddy coming, Theodore?” “At some point,” Theo says. “For six minutes.” Laney nods as though this is a reasonable number. “Mine calls on my birthday,” she says. “From a different area code every year. It’s like a game show. I try to guess the state.” Theo lifts his sparkling water an inch off his stomach, and she lifts the orange juice, and that is the whole conversation, conducted across the water between two professionals.

The iPhone rings again on the side table. Theo has it before the first ring is finished, and he’s in the Poppy voice at once: “Hey, Pops.” He listens. He smiles at the sky, a smile Jack has not seen on him before, unguarded and a little goofy. Then he sits up and holds the phone out. “She wants the Catholic.” He lies back down. “Confirmation class. Grandmother Ashby’s project. I got out of mine.”

The voice on the other end is fourteen and talks like it’s late for something. “Hi. Is this the Catholic? Theo says you’re Catholic.” Poppy Vance of La Cañada was supposed to be at confirmation class last Sunday, and again this morning, but there was the fire, and they were evacuated, and then there were families sleeping in the parish hall where the class is, and her mom said she didn’t have to go, so she didn’t. “And now it’s two in a row and Mrs. Alvarado takes attendance, like, on a clipboard.” A breath. “So does God? Take attendance?”

body.text: So this is what Theo told her yesterday he’d ask. She has gotten tired of waiting and asked herself, which seems, from what Jack has seen of the family, like the right call.

journal.title: Poppy
journal.text: Theo’s sister. Fourteen. Wants to know if God takes attendance.

choices.text: Tell her the truth, gently.
response: Jack sits on the edge of the chaise and tells her the truth, as plain as he can make it. There’s no sign-in sheet. Mrs. Alvarado has a clipboard; God has her. Go back when you can, and go back when you can’t think of a reason to, and He’s there either way, which is sort of the whole point of Him. On the other end Poppy considers this. “Okay,” she says. “Cool. Okay.” And then, “Can I ask you stuff again? Theo doesn’t know anything.”
When Theo gets the phone back and says goodbye, he lies down again with his arm over his eyes. “She’s going to ask for you now,” he says. “Every time. That’s on you.”

response.text: Margot corrected my Greek in front of Herakles. I have never been so happy. Tell Laney sunscreen. —L.

choices.text: Tell her you’re secretly a nun.
response: “The thing is, Poppy, I’m not really allowed to say this, but I’m actually a nun.” A silence in La Cañada. “Sister Jack. Order of the Sacred Espresso Machine. Your brother doesn’t know. We don’t touch anything and we take a vow of caffeine.” Poppy shrieks so loud Laney hears it from the pool. Gina’s nun joke, Jack thinks, has now crossed the entire country and been adopted by a stranger, and Gina would be furious about the royalties.
Theo takes the phone back, listens to his sister laugh for a while without saying anything, and looks at Jack over it like he’s been handed something.

response.text: Margot corrected my Greek in front of Herakles. I have never been so happy. Tell Laney sunscreen. —L.

choices.text: Say hi, and hand the phone back to her brother.
response: “Hi, Poppy. I think that’s a question for your brother.” He hands it back. Theo takes the phone to the far end of the deck, out where the rail meets the beach stairs, and stands with his back to the house. The wind brings Jack pieces of it — *no, Pops* and *I know* and *I promise* — in the Poppy voice, and then takes them away again out over the sand.

response.text: Margot corrected my Greek in front of Herakles. I have never been so happy. Tell Laney sunscreen. —L.

s10.slug: SUNDAY · 5:52 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, KITCHEN

body.text: They left the Villa at half past four. Lena brought Kevin’s van back up the PCH at a speed Kevin will not be told about, and by ten to six everybody is in the kitchen, sunburned and salt-stiff, Lena still holding the folded museum map like a ticket stub, Laney and Theo damp from the pool.
body.else: They left the Villa at half past four. At twenty to six the Odyssey comes down the drive with Lena at the wheel and Margot in the back seat holding the door handle, and by ten to six everybody is in the kitchen, Lena describing Herakles to Laney with both hands and no regard for the dignity of marble.

body.text: Jack is at the sink with the gumbo pot. It has been soaking since last night, the roux baked to a dark ring an inch below the rim, and under the terms negotiated in 412 at nine o’clock yesterday morning it is his. He has his sleeves pushed up and his hands in gray water to the wrist.
body.else: Jack is at the sink with the gumbo pot. It has been soaking since last night, the roux baked to a dark ring an inch below the rim, and nobody asked him to; the Hobart has ruined him. He can’t sit in a kitchen with a dirty pot in it. He has his sleeves pushed up and his hands in gray water to the wrist.

body: The car arrives before the man does. Up on the drive, behind the hedge, somebody has a stereo turned up loud enough to come down through the house: Steely Dan, glossy and sinister, Donald Fagen wanting to know if there’s gas in the car. Theo is at the island peeling an orange in one long spiral. He stops peeling. He looks at the clock on the stove. “That’s him,” he says, sunny. “Six minutes. Somebody time him.” Margot already has the Nokia out. Her thumb comes down. It beeps.

Richard Vance comes in through the garage door talking. He is tan in the way of a man who has never once been sunburned against his will, in a linen shirt the color of sand, reading glasses pushed up into silver-blond hair, a BlackBerry in one hand and the other free for whoever’s next. Behind him comes a woman in white jeans and gold sandals: thirty, maybe, pretty with the kind of effort that never shows on camera. “*Teddy!*” Richard gets an arm around Theo’s shoulders and squeezes and reads his BlackBerry over the top of Theo’s head while he does it. Theo stands in the hug holding the orange. His smile doesn’t go anywhere at all. “Hi, Dad. Hi, Brynn.”
Then Richard does the room. He goes around the island with his hand out — “Richard” — and each of them says a name, and he hands each name straight back, once, warm, like a good tip.

“Lena Broussard.” “*Broussard.* Like the restaurant on Conti? Best turtle soup in the Quarter. We made a picture down there after the storm. The tax credits were *obscene*.” Lena gives him the smile Jack saw her give a parking officer on the Commons Lawn the day he first laid eyes on her. “Different Broussards, sir. We’re the seafood ones. Banks Street.” “Even better,” says Richard Vance. “Real people.” Brynn has lifted the lid on the leftover gumbo on the back burner and is breathing it in with her eyes shut. “Did *you* make this? Will you give me the recipe?” Lena gives it to her, roux and all, forty-five minutes, don’t walk away, and Brynn thumbs every word into a white iPhone and says, “Rich. We’re making this.” “Inés will make it,” Richard says, already on to Laney.

body.text: He reads the front of the hoodie. “Cardinal Mooney. Is that a band?” “It’s a *lifestyle*, sir.” Richard points at her, delighted, like he might cast her in something.
body.else: He reads the front of her T-shirt. “Highland Park Lacrosse. You play?” “I *dated* it, sir.” Richard points at her, delighted, like he might cast her in something.

body: “Kevin Tran.” “Tran. We shot a picture in Vietnam — Hội An, oh-two. The river at night, the lanterns. Gorgeous country.” Kevin gives him the full floor-meeting smile. “I’ve heard it’s beautiful, sir. I’ve never been.”

“Margot Lindqvist.” She doesn’t take the hand; she has the Nokia in it. “How many people did Meridian lay off this year?” Richard doesn’t blink. “Two hundred and twelve. I kept nine hundred employed through a writers’ strike and the worst year since ’82. What’s your number?” “Name one,” says Margot. And for the first time since he came through the door Richard Vance slows down. “Denise Okafor. Story department. Nineteen years. I told her myself, in my office.” He holds Margot’s eye. “Then I went to lunch, because I had a lunch.” Margot writes it down, both halves, and doesn’t say anything, and neither does he.

“Dad,” Theo says, “and this is — ” The BlackBerry goes. Richard lifts one finger and answers it in the middle of Theo’s sentence. “No. No. Don’t call legal. Call Marty. Marty fixes it.” He hangs up. Theo’s hand, flat on the counter beside the orange peel, has stopped where it was.

Richard checks the time on the BlackBerry. “We’re due in the Colony.” And on his way back toward the garage he sees Jack — sleeves up, gray water to the wrists, the Brillo in one hand — and his face brightens like a man who’s found one more thing to take care of. “The caterer send you?” Richard has a silver money clip open before Jack’s hands are out of the water. He peels off a hundred and tucks it into the breast pocket of Jack’s flannel with two fingers. He pats it flat. “For putting up with my son.” Across the island Lena has set down the wooden spoon she was tasting from. Theo’s face is the one he wears at the end of a party, when the lights come up. Richard is already halfway to the door, thumb on the trackball.

choices.text: Hand it back: “I’m Theo’s friend, sir. Not the help.”
choices.key: You handed Richard Vance his hundred back.
response: Jack dries his hand on his jeans, takes the bill out of his pocket, and holds it out. “I’m Theo’s friend, sir. Not the help.” Richard turns around in the doorway and looks at him for the first time, really — the black hair, the broken nose, the hand held out steady with a hundred dollars in it — and laughs, a big producer’s laugh. “First friend he’s had I couldn’t tip.” He takes it back and pockets it. At the island Theo has started peeling the orange again, very slowly, as if it requires all his attention.

choices.text: “Thank you, sir.” Keep it.
choices.key: You kept Richard Vance’s hundred.
response: “Thank you, sir.” Richard is already gone. Jack dries his hands, takes *Brideshead* out of his back pocket, and folds the hundred into it a few pages past the holy card. A hundred dollars is twelve and a half hours at the Hobart. He puts the book back in his pocket. Theo watches it go into the book. Then he studies the countertop as if somebody had written on it.

choices.text: Hand it straight to Theo: “For the gas.”
choices.key: You gave Richard Vance’s hundred to Theo for the gas.
response: Jack takes the bill out of his pocket and holds it across the island to Theo. “For the gas.” Theo looks at it, and at Jack, and takes it and slides it into the front pocket of his jeans. “Under the pie,” he says. In the doorway Richard is reading something on the BlackBerry and laughing at it, and doesn’t notice that his money has gone around the kitchen and come back to his son.

choices.text: “Make it two and I’ll do the windows.”
choices.key: You talked Richard Vance up to two hundred.
response: “Make it two,” Jack says, “and I’ll do the windows.” The kitchen goes very still. Richard turns in the doorway with his eyebrows up, and then he laughs, pointing at Jack with the BlackBerry. “This one I like.” He comes back, peels a second hundred off the clip, and tucks it in on top of the first. Jack has two hundred dollars in his shirt pocket and a problem, and the problem is standing at the island holding half an orange and not looking at him.

s10b.slug: SUNDAY · 5:58 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE DECK
body: They all end up out on the deck to see him off, as if he were a relative. The Range Rover backs up the drive with Steely Dan coming out of it again. Brynn waves from the passenger side with her whole arm, a real wave, and Lena waves back. Richard doesn’t look up from the BlackBerry. The hedge closes behind them. The dinner is in the Colony.
Margot looks at the Nokia. “Six minutes, fourteen seconds.” Theo nods, his hands in his pockets, his eyes on the empty drive. “He’s slipping.”
