body: Then Laney walks up behind Theo, puts both hands flat between his shoulder blades, and shoves him into the pool in his four-hundred-dollar T-shirt.

body.text: He goes in sideways and enormous, and Richard Vance’s hundred goes in with him, in the front pocket of his jeans.
body.else: He goes in sideways and enormous, sunglasses and all.

body: He comes up laughing — a real laugh, all the way out, water streaming off his hair — and then he stops swimming and turns over and floats on his back in the middle of the pool with his arms out, in his clothes, looking straight up at the sky, smoke-yellow, one plane crossing it very high. He stays there. Nobody calls to him. The pump hums.
“Somebody had to,” Laney says, to no one, and sits down on the edge with her feet in the water.
Kevin goes inside and comes back with a towel, a big one, white, and folds it once and leaves it on the coping at the shallow end, where Theo will find it when he wants it, and goes back in.

journal.title: Richard Vance
journal.text: Theo’s father. Learned everybody’s name in one pass but mine; thought I came with the caterer. Calls him Teddy. Stayed six minutes, fourteen seconds. Margot timed it.

s11.slug: SUNDAY · 9:10 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE DECK
body: The fire pit on Richard’s deck burns gas up through blue glass, which Lena calls a sin against firewood and sits beside anyway, knees up under the cardigan, last night’s pie on the arm of her chair. A waning moon is coming up over the shoulder of the Santa Monica Mountains, orange with smoke, a day or two past full. Below the boards the Pacific is black and loud, all sound and no sight.

She sets the plate down. “Costigan.” Talk around the fire dies in stages. “I owe you a Sunday.” She looks at the moon, then back at him. “It’s Sunday.” Laney wants to know the score. “He’s up two–nothing on the season,” Lena says, pushing her sleeves to the elbow, “and I don’t care for it.”

Margot appoints herself moderator, Nokia stopwatch up. “Four rounds. Ninety seconds. I’m grading for coherence and complicity.” Laney is ring girl, with a pool noodle over one shoulder and the cardboard flap off Kevin’s case of Arrowhead, ROUND 1 in Sharpie. Kevin keeps score on his BlackBerry. Theo is still in the jeans he went into the pool in three hours ago, his hair gone stiff with chlorine. “Changing would be a concession,” he says, and rises to make a presentation.

body.text: He plucks the folded bill out of the *Brideshead* on the arm of Jack’s chair, flattens it on the teak with the side of his hand, and weights it with a citronella glass. “Exhibit A.”
He holds an empty palm up to the firelight. “Exhibit A has left the building. It’s back in my father’s pocket. He was thrilled.”
He peels a sodden hundred out of the front pocket of the jeans and lays it on the teak beside the fire, where it begins, faintly, to steam. “Exhibit A. It’s been through the pool.”
He holds out his hand until Jack surrenders the money, then fans the two hundreds on the teak like a hand of cards he intends to win with. “Exhibit A. And its little brother.”

body: Lena leans forward into the blue light, elbows on her knees, and opens.
“You were *tipped*, Costigan. How does it feel to be labor?”

s11a.slug: SUNDAY · 9:14 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE FIRE PIT
body: Laney walks the cardboard once around the fire pit in a slow pageant circuit, noodle on her shoulder like a parasol. Margot says “Go.”

Lena doesn’t need notes. She pushes her sleeves the rest of the way up and goes. “Leo the Thirteenth, *Rerum Novarum*, 1891, section forty-five. A tip is a gift. A wage is a debt. You can’t owe a man a gift, and you can’t gift him what you owe him. Leo says there’s a law older than any bargain two men can make: a wage has to be enough to keep a frugal, decent worker alive. And if need or fear makes a man take worse, he is — and I’m quoting a pope — *the victim of force and injustice*.” She points at his shirt pocket, where the money was. “Go stand at the Anchor at closing and watch the waitresses count the jar. Every dollar in it is a decision somebody made over pie about whether she’s a person tonight.”

body.text: “Two hundred dollars isn’t a wage, Costigan. It isn’t even a gift. He tipped you before he looked at you. Mr. Vance paid you like weather.”
body.else: “A hundred dollars isn’t a wage, Costigan. It isn’t even a gift. He tipped you before he looked at you. Mr. Vance paid you like weather.”

choices.text: Leo says the worker owes a fair day’s work and keeps his hands off the boss’s property. Section twenty. Justice runs both ways.
response: “You want to explain the dignity of labor to *me*? On Labor Day?” “It’s Sunday.” “It’s Labor Day *weekend*, Costigan, and I’m counting it.” She doesn’t break stride. “Granted. The Anchor’d fire you for a chipped cup and be right. Both ways, yes. It just never seems to run *uphill* on its own.” She takes the point and keeps walking with it, as if he’d handed her his coat.

choices.text: “It was the best-paid pot in the history of pots.”
response: She laughs, caught clean, and points at him across the blue glass with the laugh still on her face. “Which is my *point*. A hundred dollars for one pot is a crazy man’s number. Nobody can feed a family on crazy.” Laney applauds with the noodle.

choices.text: “It was the best-paid pot in the history of pots. Twice.”
response: She laughs, caught clean, and points at him across the blue glass with the laugh still on her face. “Which is my *point*. Two hundred dollars for one pot is a crazy man’s number. Nobody can feed a family on crazy.” Laney applauds with the noodle.

choices.text: “I was the best-paid pot in the history of pots for about four seconds.”
response: She laughs, caught clean, and points at him across the blue glass with the laugh still on her face. “And then you handed it back, which is my *point*. You could afford four seconds of pride because somebody pays you on Tuesday. The man who can’t has to say *thank you, sir*.” Laney applauds with the noodle.

choices.text: “He paid me like furniture. You’re right.”
response: She has the next paragraph loaded — he can see it lined up behind her teeth — and suddenly there’s nobody standing where she meant to hit. She closes her mouth. She looks at him differently, a half-second’s worth. Margot, unblinking, consults the Nokia. “Concession at forty-one seconds,” she says.

choices.text: Benedict wants gift *inside* the economy — gratuitousness. *Caritas in Veritate*, thirty-six. A tip is the gift.
response: “Your own pope, Broussard. July. Gratuitousness and the logic of gift have to find their place *within* normal economic activity. A tip is the gift.”

Kevin is typing a point for Broussard before she opens her mouth. “*Inside* it, Costigan.” She’s had this one loaded since July. “Not *instead* of it. Section six of the same letter: you can’t *give* a man what’s yours until you’ve given him what’s his. You don’t get to tip your way out of a wage.”

s11b.slug: SUNDAY · 9:19 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE FIRE PIT
body: ROUND 2, says the Arrowhead box, going by at knee height.

Lena turns her chair to face him square. “*Caritas in Veritate*, section twenty-five. Your pope, Costigan, your favorite, your theologian with the nice shoes — not some Jesuit in Berkeley. He says the calls the Church has made since *Rerum Novarum* for workers’ associations that can defend their rights *must therefore be honoured today even more than in the past*. Even more. In July. With the whole world falling down.” She holds up one hand. “There’s a man on Banks Street named Mr. Alcide who shucked oysters for forty-one years at a place with tablecloths. No union. When his hands went, they gave him a ham at Christmas and his stool to somebody’s nephew in January. That’s what *honoured* looks like when nobody at the table has the standing to say the word.”

body.text: She smiles, which is never good news. “And Hale called it Monday, in front of God and Yusuf. We formed a union. Are you going to bust it?”

choices.text: The Jobs Bank: men on full wages doing crosswords in a room, suspended last winter because even the UAW couldn’t defend it to Congress.
response: “It’s bingo with a pension,” Jack adds, because it’s right there. Theo, from the end of the deck: “*Ooh*.”

Lena gives him the program in one breath — indefensible, she says, and they knew it, which is why they let it go — and refuses the rest in the next. “One bad parish doesn’t refute the Church, Costigan. You of all people know that.”

choices.text: “Does Broussard’s Seafood have a union?”
response: Lena laughs so hard she has to put her pie down. “Lord, *no*. Daddy would sooner unionize the crawfish. He pays his shuckers over scale and they eat at our table on Christmas Eve, and you can quit a union.” She lets it sit, wiping her eye with a knuckle. Kevin is already scoring it. “Nobody quits a Broussard. That’s all a union is, Costigan: a family for men whose boss won’t set them a place.”

response: She grants the principle with one nod. “Pius is right. So go small. A man alone on an assembly line can’t sit across a table from General Motors; that’s the small thing failing, so you go up exactly one step. The local. The local’s a *parish*, Costigan. Your argument’s with headquarters.” She has taken his premise and walked it somewhere he didn’t send it, and Margot makes a small appreciative noise she will later deny.

body: ROUND 3. Laney holds the cardboard over her head this time, like a girl at a prizefight in a movie.

Lena doesn’t get up. “Four years ago last week my city went under, and the federal government took days to find it. Days. People on roofs writing on the shingles with house paint. The first people on Banks Street with gloves and bleach were a youth group from a parish in Minnesota, in a school bus, with a priest who’d never seen a crawfish. Not the government. *Minnesota*.” Her voice stays even; that’s how Jack knows to listen. “Then last winter Washington found — Kevin?” “Seventeen billion in December,” Kevin says, eyes on the BlackBerry. “A lot more since.” “Tens of billions for two car companies inside six months. I’m *for* it, Costigan. I’m just noting where they keep their compassion.”

Margot, unasked: “Observation. Both your parties read the encyclicals the way Theo reads a menu, for the parts they already wanted. The right takes the paragraphs on property, the left takes the paragraphs on the wage, and nobody reads the one where the Pope says they’re both wrong. Carry on.”
Jack has spent the night arguing with the part of his head that goes to Mass. The bailout isn’t in an encyclical. It’s on the kitchen table on Glenwood Avenue, and it’s been there since June.

Lena doesn’t make it a moment. She makes it an argument. “Then he knows exactly what it’s worth,” she says, “and so do you. So argue like it.” And she waits for him — Lena Broussard, in a duel, waits.

response: Lena looks at him over the fire, a long look, and then goes around him like water around a piling. “Fine. Yusuf’s father, then.” She was on the cloister walk; she heard it. “GM and Toyota built cars together in Fremont for twenty-five years. The bailout saved GM, and this summer GM walked out on Fremont, and on the twenty-seventh of August Toyota said they’re closing it. Yusuf called that job the load-bearing wall of the house. Nobody bailed out *that* wall.” She takes the round on someone else’s father, and Jack lets her have it.

s11d.slug: SUNDAY · 9:31 PM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE FIRE PIT
body: ROUND 4, and Laney, sensing the room, walks it around without a word.

Lena is quiet, which is new. Her hand goes to the gold medal at her throat and turns it once on its chain while she looks into the fire, and when she speaks she has slowed down. “John Paul. *Laborem Exercens*, section six. Work is for man, not man for work. The dignity of work lives in the one doing it, not in the job. You can’t lay that off. Mr. Alcide still has a shucker’s hands. Nobody gets to fire *those*.” She lets go of the medal.

body.text: “Your father didn’t lose his dignity in June, Costigan. General Motors lost *him*.” Then, plainly, as if she actually wants to know: “What did he make?”
body.else: “Yusuf’s father didn’t lose his dignity at NUMMI. NUMMI lost *him*.” She tilts her head. “And yours, Costigan? You’re from Youngstown, and you just skipped a round you were winning.”

choices.text: “Twenty-six years of cars. Sunday gravy. A garage you could eat off of.”
response: He hears himself say it and doesn’t take any of it back. Lena doesn’t make a joke. After a second she says, “That’s what I mean,” very quietly, and nods at Margot to call it, and wins the round looking as though she would rather have lost it.

choices.text: “Cobalts. Twenty-six years. Laid off in June. You win.”
choices.key: You told Lena about your father, and gave her the round.
response: He gives it to her flat, all of it at once, like a man emptying his pockets at a desk. Lena takes the round and doesn’t pick it up. “I didn’t want it like that,” she says. Then, honest to the last: “I’ll take it. I didn’t want it like that.”

choices.text: “Dignity doesn’t make the mortgage. A job does.”
choices.key: You lost the labor duel to Lena on her Sunday.
response: “John Paul again,” he says. “*Centesimus Annus*, forty-eight. When the State takes over what people owe each other, you get more offices and less human energy. A union can turn into that too: a pension office with a parking lot. The contract that priced Lordstown out of building cars was signed by the men you’re canonizing.” Kevin, very quietly, gives him the point.

“No. *Justice* makes the mortgage.” She’s on her feet now, the cardigan off one shoulder, the Pacific going off under the deck like applause. “And John Paul wrote that after ten years of standing behind a union with ten million members in Gdańsk, Costigan. Read the whole paragraph.” Laney thumps the noodle on the boards three times. “That’s why I’m for the union, and so are you. You’ll just vote like you’re not.”

response: She laughs into her sleeve and points at him with the other hand until she can talk, and wins the round anyway. “Thursday’s fine. Tell him he can pick it up at the union hall. They’re open late.”

response: The fire hisses. Lena sets her plate down on the deck carefully, so that it makes no sound at all. She is polite. Every consonant is in its place.
“Broussard’s took five feet of water, Mr. Costigan. My daddy and his brothers rebuilt it with their hands. The house too.”
Nothing more.

body: Margot stops the Nokia. Kevin reads off the BlackBerry like a man announcing a birth: “Broussard. That’s two–one on the season.”

body.text: She wins, and she is gracious about it. She thanks the moderator and the ring girl, and she is perfectly pleasant to Mr. Costigan for two more hours, which he wouldn’t wish on anyone. At midnight, crossing behind his chair on her way in, she drops a dry towel on his head without breaking stride. It’s as close to forgiveness as tonight is going to get.

She wins and won’t take it. “We’re even, Youngstown,” she says, which by Kevin’s count they are not, and nobody corrects her. Later she cuts the last slice of the peach pie, sets it on the arm of his chair without a word, and goes back around to her side of the fire.

She wins on points. She stands, rolls her sleeves back down one at a time, and steals Hale’s line with the boredom and the cut glass both: “That was very nearly an argument, Costigan.” Margot, consulting the Nokia: “Broussard, by a minute forty.” Kevin, consulting his columns: “You took every point, Costigan. She took the room.”

She wins, and Laney rises from her chaise and crowns her Miss Congeniality, bending the pool noodle into a hoop on her head, and teaches her the pageant wave on the spot. “Wrist, wrist, elbow, elbow. Smile like your daddy’s in the front row, sugar.” Lena does it at the Pacific, perfectly, to a standing ovation from Theo, who stays seated. “The judges liked your jokes,” Margot tells Jack, “and her logic.”
Margot calls it for Broussard, on coherence. Lena accepts with a magnanimous hand. “Put it on the board, Kevin.” “There’s no board.” “There will be,” says Margot.

Later, when the others have gone in, Lena asks him one plain question across the fire. “Is he okay?” “He’s good.” She looks at him over the blue glass as if she’s weighing the word. Then she lets him keep it.

s12.slug: MONDAY · 7:12 AM · THE VANCE HOUSE, KITCHEN
body: Labor Day comes in gray. The marine layer has the beach again, pressed to the glass, and the house is quiet enough that Jack can hear the refrigerator’s compressor and, under it, the surf. He’s at the sink with last night’s glasses, because there are glasses and there is a sink: wine glasses from the fire pit with a red line dried in the bottom of each, a coffee mug of Margot’s, two Arrowhead bottles.

Theo is at the island in the navy silk robe from the fire alarm, with an espresso and his hair flattened on one side. He has picked up a dish towel from somewhere and is drying one wine glass, slowly, turning it in the towel as if he’s read about this. “I slept,” he says, though Jack hasn’t asked. “Eleven-forty to six-fifty. Left side. I dreamed about Rossellini.” Jack doesn’t say anything. Theo turns the glass.

The RAZR buzzes on the counter by the coffee, rattling against the marble. A number Jack doesn’t have saved, long, out of state. The screen only lights when he tips it. He dries his hand on his jeans and opens it to a recording, a woman’s voice, flat and loud in the quiet kitchen: “This is a prepaid call from — ” and then a gap, and into the gap a voice Jack knows better than his own, saying its own name: “*Danny.*” And the woman again: “ — an inmate at Trumbull Correctional Institution. This call is from a correctional facility and is subject to monitoring and recording. To accept this call, press — ”
Theo is three feet away with the towel in one hand and the glass in the other. Jack presses the key.

“*Professor.*” There it is: Glenwood Avenue in a voice, gravel and laughing, a little out of breath like he just came in from somewhere. “You up? It’s ten o’clock. Ma put money on it, so don’t make me talk to myself.” Jack says, “I’m up,” and his voice works. Behind Danny there’s a room full of other men’s voices and a television and a door that buzzes and bangs. “Ma came yesterday. Brought the good socks. The gray ones, the wool. Spent ten minutes at the desk telling the C.O. they’re not contraband, they’re *socks*. She won.” A laugh. “She says there’s a veil girl.” “There’s a girl in my class who wears a veil to Mass.” “That’s what I said, Professor. A veil girl.”

body.text: “And you wash dishes. Dad told her. *Dad* told her.” Danny lets that sit, so Jack can hear how big it is. “Dad don’t tell her nothing. So he’s proud. So don’t be a pussy about it.”
“Dad says you wrote. It ain’t come.” “Thursday. I mailed it Thursday.” “Mail’s slow in here. They read it first. Some guy in the mailroom’s gonna know your business before me.”

body: The tap is still running. Jack doesn’t turn it off. His free hand has found the St. Michael medal through his T-shirt and is holding it, the edge of it pressing into his thumb. “Where are you?” Danny says. “It sounds like money.” Jack looks at the kitchen: the steel, the glass, the Carrara, the gray ocean past the glass, Theo standing in all of it in a silk robe drying one glass forever. “Malibu.” “Get *out*.” A whoop, and somebody on Danny’s end tells him to keep it down, and he says something back Jack can’t hear. Then he’s close to the phone again, and quieter. “Describe it.”

choices.text: Describe the ocean, plainly.
response: So he does. He turns to the glass and tells his brother what’s there. It’s gray right now, with fog lying on it low. Under the fog it’s green close in and blue farther out, and there’s a line where it meets the sky that you can’t find, you keep looking and you can’t. It’s cold, colder than Lake Glacier in May. The house is right on top of it, and all night you can hear it under the floor, coming in and going out, like somebody breathing in the next room.
On the other end nobody says anything. The television, the door buzzing. Then Danny, quiet: “Okay. Okay.” A breath. “Keep that one.”

choices.text: Describe Malibu as a crime scene: the labeled fridge, the Oscar by the toilet.
response: “Okay. Victim’s a refrigerator. Every container in it labeled, same handwriting: R.V., Monday, Do Not. Do not *what*, Danny. It doesn’t say. We have no suspects. Then you go down the hall to take a leak, and there’s an Academy Award on the shelf next to the hand towels. A real one. I picked it up. It weighs about what a kid’s bowling ball weighs.”

And Danny is laughing — the big one, from the stomach, the one that used to come up the stairs on Glenwood at two in the morning when he thought everybody was asleep, the one Jack hasn’t heard since — and Jack keeps talking so it won’t stop. The Oscar has a little gold sword. The man who owns the Oscar has a hedge cut with a ruler. Danny laughs until somebody on his end tells him to shut up, and he tells them to shut up, and keeps laughing.

choices.text: Hand the phone to Theo: “Say hi to my brother.”
choices.key: You let Theo talk to Danny.
response: Jack holds the RAZR out across the counter. “Say hi to my brother.” Theo looks at the phone. Then he puts the glass down and takes it, dish towel and all, and puts it to his ear, and the earpiece is loud enough in the quiet kitchen that Jack hears both halves.

“Who’s this?” “The roommate.” “He any good?” Theo looks at Jack over the phone for a second. “He’s a menace.” Danny laughs, low. “Yeah. He is.” Then, in a different voice, the one he used to use at the top of the driveway when Jack was nine and going somewhere on a bike: “Look out for him.” Theo doesn’t say anything clever. He hands the phone back.

body: The recorded woman cuts in over whatever Danny is saying: “You have one minute remaining.” Danny talks faster. “Go to Mass. Eat something. Don’t be a pussy, Professor. Tell the veil girl I said — ”

And then it’s a dial tone, steady and stupid, in a kitchen in Malibu. Jack holds the RAZR to his ear until the dial tone becomes the other noise, the one that tells you to hang up, and then he closes it. He reaches over and turns off the tap.

Theo hasn’t moved. Jack has watched Theo fill every silence on the fourth floor of Delgado Hall for a week — with a pitch, a logline, a story about a director, a bottle — and he doesn’t fill this one. He doesn’t ask what Danny did. He stands at the island in the silk robe with the gray light on him and waits, which Jack has never once seen him do.

response: “He’s in Trumbull,” Jack says. “It’s a state prison, outside Warren. Five years. A fight — a guy got hurt bad. He pleaded. Three more to go, maybe less.” It’s what his mother says at St. Brigid’s when anybody asks, and he says it the same way she does, and stops.

Theo asks one question. “What does he read?” “Whatever I send.” Theo nods, as if that answers something he’d been wondering about for a while, and folds the dish towel in thirds and lays it on the counter.

response: “He’s at a very exclusive school in Ohio,” Jack says. “Hard to get into. Harder to get out of.” Theo leaves the joke where it is. “Then I’ll send an application fee.” And then, short, with nothing on it: “I heard the recording, Costigan. It’s okay. I’m nobody.”

response: “Don’t tell anybody,” Jack says. “Not yet.” Theo looks at him across the island. “I’m good at that.” A pause. “Better than you’d think.” He picks up his espresso, finds it cold, and drinks it.

The Browns are a long-term investment.” “Aw,” says Laney, with real sympathy. “Sugar.” She pats Jack’s arm on her way past, opens the refrigerator, considers the R.V. containers, closes it, and takes a peach from the bowl instead, satisfied in every particular.

Jack takes the cup. He takes the Marlboros out of the Carhartt on the back of the stool. He goes out through the glass door and across the deck, past the pool with the towel still folded on the coping, to the top of the beach stairs, where the fog is starting to come apart.

s13.slug: MONDAY · 8:05 AM · THE VANCE HOUSE, THE BEACH STAIRS
body: By eight the marine layer is lifting off Broad Beach in pieces, and the light coming through it has no shadows in it, like the inside of a shell. Jack sits on the weathered stairs below the deck with Theo’s espresso on the step beside him and the Marlboros open on his knee. He has been not lighting one for the life of an espresso. The RAZR is in his pocket, folded shut.
*Describe it*, Danny said. It’s gray this morning. He’d have to start there.

Behind him the screen door slides, and Lena comes down the stairs: a navy one-piece that has clearly had a life before her, the oatmeal cardigan over it, unbuttoned, a striped towel over one shoulder, her Keds hooked on one finger. The tin is in the cardigan pocket. She is soft and gold and entirely at ease in her own skin at eight in the morning, and Jack, who was raised right and is not made of wood, looks at the ocean.
She stops two steps above him and looks at the pack, the cup, his face. She doesn’t ask. Whatever she sees there, she stands on the step with it a moment.

choices.text: Light it anyway.
choices.key: You gave Lena’s reliquary its second relic.
response: He lights it. He gets the first drag, the one that goes all the way down to the place it’s for, and then her hand is there and the cigarette isn’t, and she’s stubbing it out on the step between his feet as if she’s done it all her life. The tin comes out of the cardigan with a little hinge-click, the Lighthouse cigarette lying in it on its bed of paper, and she lays No. 2 beside it, uncaps a pen with her teeth, and writes the slip against her bare knee.

response.title: A slip of paper, folded into the tin
response.text: No. 2 · 9/7/09 · Malibu · before breakfast, on a holiday.

response: He closes the lid and puts the pack in his back pocket, behind the *Brideshead*, before she’s off the last step. She sees it go. She sits down beside him with a thump, digs the tin out of her cardigan and shakes it at him, one lonely cigarette sliding end to end inside like a bead in a rattle. “I brought the tin and *everything*.”

response: He shakes one out and holds it up to her, filter first. “For the collection.” She looks at it, and at him, and doesn’t take it. “Donations aren’t relics, Costigan. They’re *tithes*.” Then her own line from the Hollis steps, in mint condition: “Where’s the sport?” She takes his wrist instead — the hand with the cigarette in it — and pulls him down the last step onto the cold sand.

s13b.slug: MONDAY · 8:20 AM · BROAD BEACH, THE WATER’S EDGE
body: Down at the water the sand is packed hard and cold under their feet, and the beach belongs to them, a man with a golden retriever a quarter mile east, and the gulls. Lena drops the towel, folds the cardigan on top of it with the tin inside, and stands with her toes on the line where the foam gives up.

“Sixty-six degrees,” she says. “Kevin looked it up for me this morning, on his BlackBerry, and then he looked at *me* like I’d asked him to look up my obituary.” She regards the Pacific with deep personal suspicion. “This is the Gulf’s mean cousin. The one who went off to boarding school and came back talking funny.”

body.text: She hasn’t called him anything yet this morning: not Costigan, not Youngstown, not Mr. anything. Whatever she’s saving it for, she’s still saving it.

body: Then she looks at him instead, properly, with her red-pen face on. “You look like somebody’s Monday.”

choices.text: “Family stuff. It’s good, actually. Mostly.”
response: She doesn’t push. She looks at him a second more and lets it be exactly what he said it was. “Okay.” Then she nods at the water. “Then you need the Pacific. It’s a sacrament for Protestants.”

choices.text: “The Browns.”
response: “Lord.” She puts a hand on his arm in sympathy, briefly, as at a wake. “That’s a *grief*. Get in the water.”

choices.text: “Race you.” And go.
response: He’s off before the words are out, and she’s past him by the second stride, because she has put a hand in the middle of his back going by and shoved. “*Cheater*.” “*Catholic*,” she yells, and hits the water first.

choices.text: “I was out of line last night. About your father. Your family.”
choices.key: You apologized to Lena for what you said about her family.
response: She looks at him for a long moment with the Pacific going over behind her. “Apology noted, Mr. Costigan.” Then she turns to the water and wades in to the knee, and says over her shoulder, without looking back, “Costigan. Get in. It’s worse if you wait.”

s13c.slug: MONDAY · 8:24 AM · BROAD BEACH, THE WATER
body: The cold takes his breath at the knees and the rest of it at the waist. Lena goes under once and comes up shrieking, hair streaming, swearing by saints she invents on the spot — Saint Frigidaire, abbot; Blessed Somebody of the Icebox — and Jack laughs so hard he takes in a mouthful of the Pacific.

Then a wave stands up out of nowhere, green and glassy along the top, and breaks across both of them, and she comes off her feet straight into him. He catches her by the elbows. For a second they’re chest-deep in the Pacific holding on, her hands flat on his forearms, salt caught in her eyelashes, his St. Michael gone cold against his sternum, both of them laughing too hard to stand up properly. He can feel the whole cold ocean except for the few inches where she is. He knows exactly what the next second is. He has known since a porch light went out on Seacliff Road.
He lets go first.

His hands keep the shape of her elbows for a while under the water, and the ocean is very cold, and he minds both of those things a great deal. Then she ducks under and comes up streaming and yells at the sky about it, and he’s laughing again, and the laughing is the realest thing that has happened to him since the phone buzzed on the marble. She lies back and floats with her arms out and her hair fanned on the swell, and gives the gray sky the Who Dat at full volume, *who dat say dey gonna beat dem Saints*, to an audience of one golden retriever, who barks back.

Jack treads water and starts the letter in his head. *Sixty-six degrees. Green at the top of the waves, gray underneath. It sounds like a truck going by that never finishes going by. A girl from New Orleans hates it.*

Out of the water she wraps herself in the cardigan, teeth going, wet wool and salt, and stands over him where he’s collapsed on the towel, and delivers her review of the Pacific Ocean. “Four out of ten. Like your marionberry.” “My dad would complain.” “About the ocean?” “About the rating. He’d give it a three. He gives everything a three.” “Your daddy,” Lena says, dripping on him, “would be *right*.”

body.text: She sits down beside him on the towel, knees up, and adds, lightly, to the water, that she’d like to meet a man who’d give the whole Pacific Ocean a three. She leaves it there. So does he.

body: Up on the deck Kevin appears at the rail waving a spatula over his head, which means breakfast. The marine layer is burning off from the east. Neither of them moves yet.

s14.slug: MONDAY · 1:10 PM · US-101 NORTH, THE ODYSSEY
body: They left Broad Beach at noon. Everyone is in the van except Theo, who is in the SL, and Laney, who at the bottom of the drive handed Kevin her three suitcases one by one and climbed into the two-seater beside Theo. “A girl can arrive in a minivan, sugar,” she told Kevin, tying a scarf over her hair. “She *leaves* in somebody’s car.” On the back glass of the Odyssey, in shoe polish, the countdown says 6 DAYS. Lena did it in the drive this morning with her wet hair dripping on the bumper.

At one o’clock Kevin switched over to KNX for the news, and they all heard it: the President in Cincinnati this morning, at the AFL-CIO’s Labor Day picnic, talking about health care and the unions and the dignity of work, and a crowd behind him that sounded, through the static on the Oxnard plain, like a parish festival when the band comes on. Then Kevin plugged in his iPod and put on Springsteen: the early-morning whistle, the men walking out in the morning light. “My dad likes the Boss,” Kevin says now, eyes on the road, ten and two. “He thinks he’s a Republican.”

Jack laughs, and Kevin looks pleased, and then, still watching the road: “My dad’s stores are open today. He has two. Nail-salon supply, in San Jose — polish, acetone, the chairs. He’s never had a Labor Day.” Kevin shrugs with one shoulder. “He says Labor Day is for people with bosses.” It’s the most Kevin has ever said about his father, and he says it the way he says everything, sunny, at sixty-five miles an hour, and then he changes lanes.
